title: Romans 2:1–11
context: After exposing Gentile ungodliness and the handing-over of 1:18–32, Paul turns to the moralist who judges those sins while practicing them. God’s kindness, forbearance, and patience are meant to lead to repentance; a hard and impenitent heart stores wrath. He will render to everyone according to their works, the Jew first, and also to the Greek. For there is no partiality.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Judging others, the kindness of God meant to lead to repentance, and judgment according to works without partiality: older Arminian and Reformed writers, each in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Or despisest thou—Dost thou go farther still, from hoping to escape his wrath, to the abuse of his love. The riches—the abundance of his goodness, forbearance, and longsuffering, seeing thou both hast sinned, dost sin, and wilt sin. Leadeth thee—that is, is designed of God to lead or encourage thee to it. For there is no respect of persons with God: he will reward every one according to his works. But this is well consistent with his distributing advantages and opportunities of improvement, according to his own good pleasure.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Romans 2:4, 11)

reformed.quote: Dost thou despise the riches? Where then the fear of God does not rule, confidence, on account of prosperity, is a contempt and a mockery of his great goodness. For the Lord by his kindness shows to us that it is he to whom we ought turn, if we desire to secure our wellbeing, and at the same time he strengthens our confidence in expecting mercy. If we use not God’s bounty for this end, we abuse it. The Lord, by visiting the wickedness of the reprobate with just vengeance, will recompense them with what they have deserved: and as he sanctifies those whom he has previously resolved to glorify, he will also crown their good works, but not on account of any merit. It is an absurd inference, to deduce merit from reward. There is no respect of persons with God: he regards purity of heart or inward integrity, and hath no respect for kindred, country, dignity, wealth, and similar things.

verses.text: Therefore you are without excuse, O man, whoever you are who judge. For in that which you judge another, you condemn yourself. For you who judge practice the same things.
verses.arminianNotes:
Therefore you are without excuse, O man, whoever you are who judge. The ’therefore’ looks back to the Gentile catalog of 1:18–32 and turns on the moralist who condemns it while walking in the same sins. In that which you judge another, you condemn yourself. Wesley’s later word (v. 4) names the next step: from hoping to escape wrath to the abuse of love.

Wesleyan Arminians take this as pastoral, not tribal. The hypocrite’s verdict on the neighbor is a verdict on himself. Both camps refuse a cheap moralism that would shelter in comparison. The gospel will soon justify the ungodly; this chapter first shuts the mouth that would excuse itself by condemning others.
verses.reformedNotes:
Therefore you are without excuse. Calvin’s later word fits the scene: where the fear of God does not rule, confidence is a contempt and a mockery of goodness. The judge who practices the very same things has no shelter in his verdict on the Gentile. God’s judgment, not ours, is the bar that matters.

This is not a license never to name sin; it is a warning that the one who sits in judgment while walking in the same sins is already self-condemned. God will not be used as a mascot for our comparisons. The ’O man’ is every moralist, Jew or Greek, who would hide behind a pointing finger.

verses.text: We know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who practice such things.
verses.arminianNotes:
We know that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who practice such things. The ’such things’ are the sins just named. Wesley will soon say there is no respect of persons with God: he will reward every one according to his works. The standard is God’s, and it is right.

Wesleyan Arminians take the rightness of this judgment with full seriousness. Kindness in v. 4 is not a denial of wrath; it is the patience of a God who still judges truly. No camp may soften ’rightly falls.’ The question is not whether God judges, but whether the one who judges others has any exemption.
verses.reformedNotes:
We know—this is shared knowledge, not a private theory—that the judgment of God is according to truth against those who practice such things. Calvin: the Lord will visit the wickedness of the reprobate with just vengeance and recompense them with what they have deserved. The sentence is righteous because God is righteous.

’rightly’ shuts every complaint against the bar. Judgment is not mood or tribal preference. Those who practice such things are under a just sentence, whether they have a Gentile resume or a Jewish one. God’s judgment is the one that stands.

verses.text: Do you think this, O man who judges those who practice such things, and do the same, that you will escape the judgment of God?
verses.arminianNotes:
Do you think this, O man who judges those who practice such things, and do the same, that you will escape the judgment of God? The supposed escape is the moralist’s last fiction. Wesley: from hoping to escape his wrath one may go farther still, to the abuse of his love. There is no escape by comparison.

Arminians catch a sincere warning: the judge who does the same things will not slip the bar. Escape is not offered to the self-excusing. God’s judgment is serious, and the kindness that follows (v. 4) is meant to lead to repentance, not to underwrite a theory that some sinners are too refined to face it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Do you suppose that you will escape the judgment of God? Calvin: where the fear of God does not rule, confidence on account of prosperity is a contempt and a mockery of his great goodness. The question expects no. The man who judges and does the same will not slip through.

There is no caste of people too religious, too instructed, or too severe on others to come under this judgment. Escape is God’s to grant in the gospel that follows; it is not the wage of a comparing conscience. The bar will hold.

verses.text: Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?
verses.arminianNotes:
Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance? Wesley: despisest thou—dost thou go farther still, from hoping to escape his wrath, to the abuse of his love. Leadeth thee: that is, is designed of God to lead or encourage thee to it. The riches are abundance; the design is repentance.

The emphasis is on a design: kindness is meant to lead, and it can be abused. Presuming on the riches is resisting a love that actually aimed at turning the sinner. Kindness is not indifference and not a trap. It is God’s chosen means to lead; the hard heart that will not be led (v. 5) is responsible for that refusal, not for a kindness that never meant him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Or do you despise the riches of his kindness? Calvin: dost thou despise the riches? Where the fear of God does not rule, confidence on account of prosperity is a contempt and a mockery of his great goodness. The Lord by his kindness shows that it is he to whom we ought to turn, if we desire to secure our wellbeing, and at the same time he strengthens our confidence in expecting mercy. If we use not God’s bounty for this end, we abuse it.

Goodness is truly kindness, and it is abused when not used to turn. The verse names the sinner’s ignorance and contempt, not a frustrated design that failed because God could not lead. Kindness is meant to lead; the heart that will not be led stores wrath. Bounty unused for repentance is bounty mocked.
verses.keyContrast: Both take the riches of kindness, forbearance, and patience as and both refuse to treat delay as permission. Arminians hear kindness designed of God to lead to repentance—a love that can be abused and resisted. Reformed Christians typically hear the same kindness as bounty meant to turn us, abused when not used to that end: contempt of goodness, not a design that finally depends on our letting it succeed.

verses.text: But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart you are treasuring up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath, revelation, and of the righteous judgment of God,
verses.arminianNotes:
But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart you are treasuring up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath, revelation, and of the righteous judgment of God, who will be revealed. The kindness of v. 4 was designed to lead to repentance; the hard heart refuses it. Wesley’s ’abuse of his love’ is not a small discourtesy. It stores wrath.

Arminian readers take storing wrath as the sinner’s own doing. Impenitence is true; the day of wrath is grave; the judgment revealed will be righteous. Kindness was meant to lead. Those who will not be led do not find that God’s patience cancelled the bar; they find they have been stacking judgment against themselves.
verses.reformedNotes:
But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart you are treasuring up for yourself wrath in the day of wrath. Calvin: the Lord will visit the wickedness of the reprobate with just vengeance. The day of wrath is the revealing of a judgment already righteous, not the birth of a mood. Hardness is the heart’s; the store is wrath.

Impenitence is not a puzzle God failed to solve with more kindness. It is the heart that will not turn, storing what the day will reveal. Righteous judgment will be public. Those whom He has resolved to glorify He also sanctifies (v. 6); the impenitent face a vengeance they have deserved.

verses.text: who “will pay back to everyone according to their works:”
verses.arminianNotes:
He will render to everyone according to their works. Wesley: he will reward every one according to his works. This is not a Pelagian ladder into first acceptance. It is the public rendering that matches a life—whether that life answered kindness with repentance or stored wrath. Judgment according to works is no empty threat; merit as the meritorious cause of justification is not what this verse teaches.

Classical Arminians refuse ’saved by works’ as the ground of pardon as heartily as any Calvinist. Works here are the way a life shows itself at the bar. God’s rendering is according to works; the gospel that follows will still justify the ungodly by grace through faith. Do not flatten Paul into a wage-system, and do not empty this verse of an according-to-works judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
He will render to everyone according to their works. Calvin: the Lord, by visiting the wickedness of the reprobate with just vengeance, will recompense them with what they have deserved; and as he sanctifies those whom he has previously resolved to glorify, he will also crown their good works, but not on account of any merit. Nor can this be proved from this verse: though it declares what reward good works are to have, it does not show what they are worth. It is an absurd inference to deduce merit from reward.

Works are the evidence of those God resolved to glorify, and the just desert of the reprobate. Reward names what good works will have; it does not price them as the cause of life. The crown is grace; the vengeance is just.
verses.keyContrast: Both take rendering according to works with full seriousness, and both refuse a Pelagian ’saved by works’ as the meritorious cause of life. Arminians typically hear works as the public evidence of a life that answered or refused kindness—reward according to works, not pardon earned by them. Reformed readers hear the same rendering, with good works crowned in those God previously resolved to glorify, not on account of merit: it is absurd to deduce merit from reward.

verses.text: to those who by perseverance in well-doing seek for glory, honor, and incorruptibility, eternal life;
verses.arminianNotes:
To those who by perseverance in well-doing seek for glory, honor, and incorruptibility, God will give eternal life. Wesley’s reward according to works is here the gift of life to a seeking, patient well-doing. This is the life of those who, by grace, persist—not a wage that purchases first justification, but the end God has appointed for well-doing.

Arminian readers find a well-doing, enabled by grace, that God will honor with eternal life. Patience in well-doing is not a meritorious climb into pardon; it is the path of those who have not presumed on kindness but have been led toward repentance. Seek glory, honor, and immortality from God, not a boast before Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
To those who by perseverance in well-doing seek for glory, honor, and incorruptibility, God will give eternal life. Calvin: as he sanctifies those whom he has previously resolved to glorify, he will also crown their good works, but not on account of any merit. The seekers of this verse are the sanctified; the life is a crown, not a price they paid.

Eternal life is given. The well-doing comes from those He resolved to glorify, not the cause that moved Him to resolve it. Patience in well-doing is no illusion, and it will be crowned. Deduce merit from that crown and the inference is absurd. Glory, honor, and immortality remain gifts of the God who sanctifies.
verses.keyContrast: Both hear eternal life given to those who by perseverance in well-doing seek glory, honor, and immortality. Arminians hear graciously enabled well-doing as the life God rewards—not a meritorious purchase of first pardon. Reformed commentators hear the good works of those He previously resolved to glorify, crowned, not on account of merit.

verses.text: but to those who are self-seeking and don’t obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, will be wrath, indignation,
verses.arminianNotes:
But to those who are self-seeking and don’t obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, will be wrath, indignation, oppression, and fury. The opposite of patient well-doing is not a small delay; it is self-seeking that will not obey the truth. Wesley’s abuse of love ends here, not in a milder court.

Classical Arminians take wrath and fury as honestly as they take kindness. Those who will not be led to repentance, who obey unrighteousness, meet a serious judgment. Self-seeking is the refusal of the truth the kindness was meant to serve. No partiality will shelter it (v. 11).
verses.reformedNotes:
To those who are self-seeking and don’t obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness, will be wrath, indignation, oppression, and fury. Calvin: the Lord, visiting the wickedness of the reprobate with just vengeance, will recompense them with what they have deserved. Wrath here is not excess; it is desert.

Self-seeking names the life that will not obey the truth. Fury is the public face of a judgment already just. The reprobate are recompensed; they are not mishandled. This verse will not be turned into a small warning. God renders; He does not negotiate the wages of unrighteousness.

verses.text: oppression, and anguish on every soul of man who does evil, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
verses.arminianNotes:
Oppression and anguish will come on every soul of man who does evil, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek. The order matches 1:16—Jew first, then Greek—now as judgment, not as a narrower mercy. Wesley: there is no respect of persons with God. Doing evil is the issue, not the badge.

Arminians hear a sincere impartiality: every soul of man who does evil meets tribulation, without a Jewish exemption or a Gentile afterthought. ’First’ is historical honor and historical accountability, not a smaller or larger gospel. Both camps must say this together before they dispute how grace saves.
verses.reformedNotes:
Tribulation and distress for every soul of man who does evil, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek. Calvin: there is no respect of persons with God; He regards purity of heart or inward integrity, and hath no respect for kindred, country, dignity, wealth. The Jew’s priority is not a shield.

’every human being’ levels the field so that no nation, rank, or rite can buy off the bar. Jew first means the people entrusted with the oracles are first at the bar as well as first in the offer. Doing evil draws distress. Kindred will not help.

verses.text: But glory, honor, and peace go to every man who does good, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
verses.arminianNotes:
But glory, honor, and peace go to every man who does good, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek. The positive twin of v. 9. Wesley: he will reward every one according to his works; this is well consistent with his distributing advantages and opportunities of improvement according to his own good pleasure. Doing good is honored; it is not a private Jewish wage.

Arminians find a reward of well-doing, Jew and Greek, without partiality. Doing good is the fruit of a life led toward repentance, not a Pelagian climb that purchases first pardon. Glory, honor, and peace come from God to everyone who does good—the same wideness as the tribulation of v. 9, and the same refusal of a badge that would replace the life.
verses.reformedNotes:
Glory, honor, and peace go to every man who does good, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek. Calvin: He crowns the good works of those He has previously resolved to glorify, but not on account of any merit. The doer of good is the sanctified person; the glory is a crown, not a price.

’everyone who does good’ is as wide in kinds as v. 9—Jew and Greek—and as particular in persons as those He sanctifies. Do not deduce merit from this peace. The same God who shows no partiality of kindred shows no weakness in grace: He gives the crown to the works He first worked.

verses.text: For there is no partiality with God.
verses.arminianNotes:
For there is no partiality. Wesley: there is no respect of persons with God—he will reward every one according to his works. But this is well consistent with his distributing advantages and opportunities of improvement according to his own good pleasure. Impartial judgment does not mean identical gifts; it means no favorite caste at the bar.

What comes through is a pastoral comfort and a pastoral threat together. The Jew is not safer by blood; the Greek is not safer by ignorance. God may distribute opportunities as He pleases; He will not judge by faces. Kindness meant to lead to repentance (v. 4) was never a private kindness for a protected class.
verses.reformedNotes:
For there is no partiality. Calvin: understand that what He regards is purity of heart or inward integrity; He hath no respect for those things highly valued by men—kindred, country, dignity, wealth, and similar things. The bar looks at the heart, not the resume.

No partiality means God will not be bribed by ancestry, passport, rank, or purse. He regards inward integrity. The reprobate are recompensed as they deserve; the sanctified are crowned without merit. Jew and Greek stand at one bar, and the gospel that follows will be the power of God for both.
